#10422. Top 6 AI Image Generators in 2026: Features, Strengths, and Limits

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

A designer who once spent an afternoon searching stock libraries can now describe the picture they want and have four versions in under a minute. AI image generators have moved from curiosity to everyday tool for blog headers, product mockups, ad concepts, game art and slide decks. The quality gap between tools has narrowed, but the differences that remain matter a lot: how well each follows a detailed prompt, whether it can render readable text, how it handles edits, and what you are allowed to do with the result.

This guide compares six of the best-known options, what each does well and where each falls short. Models, plans and limits change often, so check each vendor's own pages before you commit to a workflow.

OpenArt’s AI image generator puts several image models behind one interface. Its generator page lists models including GPT Image 2.5, Grok Imagine, Qwen Image 3, Nano Banana 2 and Seedream 5.0 Pro, and lets you create images from text prompts or reference photos. It also lists tools for camera angle control, upscaling, collages and a Character Builder for keeping characters consistent across scenes, with 4K export.

Best for: Creators who want to compare several models on the same prompt without juggling separate subscriptions and accounts.

Limitations: The page offers a free start but does not state credit amounts or plan details, and it does not address commercial use, so check the pricing and licensing pages before using results for client work. Output quality depends on which model you pick.

OpenAI's image generation in ChatGPT works inside the chat interface, which makes iteration natural: generate an image, then ask for changes in plain language. OpenAI highlights accurate text rendering, the ability to follow prompts with many distinct objects, and consistent characters across multi-turn edits. You can also upload reference images and have the model transform them. It handles both photorealistic and stylized looks.

Best for: Marketers and writers who want to describe, refine and re-describe an image without learning a new tool.

Limitations: OpenAI notes that tall images such as posters can be cropped too tightly, and that dense small text, multilingual text and precise graphs can still go wrong. Images can take up to a minute to render. All generated images carry C2PA metadata identifying their source.

Gemini's image generation runs on Google's Nano Banana models. Google highlights character consistency, text rendering in many languages, combining several photos, precise editing and 2K resolution. A free tier covers image generation and editing, while the most advanced model requires a Google AI plan. You start from the "Create images" option in the Gemini app, then prompt or upload a picture to edit.

Best for: People who need to keep the same subject across several images, or who want to edit existing photos quickly.

Limitations: Usage limits apply, and the strongest model is behind a paid plan. Images include an invisible SynthID watermark and a visible AI label, which is good for transparency but may not suit every use.

Midjourney is an independent research lab known for images with a strong, painterly look. Its official site points users to a sign-up flow and to a Discord community and help center for support. Many creators choose it for concept art, mood boards and illustration where style matters more than literal accuracy.

Best for: Artists, art directors and game designers who want rich, stylized results and enjoy exploring variations.

Limitations: I could not confirm current pricing, trial terms or feature details from Midjourney's public pages, so check them yourself before subscribing. The workflow can feel less like a normal app than the others on this list, and it is not the easiest route for precise, text-heavy graphics.

Adobe Firefly is built for professionals who already work in Creative Cloud. Adobe states that its Firefly models are commercially safe, trained on licensed Adobe Stock and public domain content, and outputs carry Content Credentials that show AI involvement. It offers text-to-image, image-to-image, sketch-to-image and style transfer, plus editing tools such as background removal, object removal, upscaling and generative expand. It connects with Photoshop, Illustrator, Lightroom and Adobe Express, and also lets you use partner models from other companies.

Best for: Designers and brand teams who need clear licensing and want AI inside the apps they already use.

Limitations: Plans work on a credit system, so heavy use adds up. Adobe lists a free tier with limited daily generations and paid plans starting at about $9.99 a month, but confirm current terms on its site.

Ideogram built its reputation on a problem that trips up many generators: readable text. Its current models are presented as producing clean typography in different layouts, with attention to prompt fidelity and reliable editing. It also offers an API with access to a catalog of models, and has released open weights for one earlier model for local use and customization under its license.

Best for: Posters, social graphics, logo concepts and anything where words are part of the image.

Limitations: The pages I checked did not describe a free plan, so look at current plans before relying on it. Like every generator, it still needs a human to proofread the text it produces.

Start with the job. If you want to compare several models side by side, try OpenArt. If you want to talk your way to a finished image, try ChatGPT or Gemini. If you need images that will sit inside a branded design workflow, Firefly is the safer fit. If you are chasing a distinctive look, Midjourney deserves a trial. If text must be perfect, test Ideogram.

Run the same prompt in two or three tools before paying. Differences in composition, hands, faces and text show up quickly, and they matter more than any feature list.

Reviews only go so far, because your own use case is what counts. Pick one realistic job, for example a 16:9 header image for a blog post about web performance, and run the same prompt through two or three tools. Write the prompt once and paste it unchanged, so the comparison is fair:

Then score each result on five questions: Did it follow every instruction? Are there odd details in hands, edges or objects? Is any text spelled correctly? Does it still look good when cropped to a square? Could you license it for your project? Ten minutes of this teaches more than any feature list, and it shows how much editing each tool needs before you can publish.

Most readers of this guide will put these images on web pages, where a few habits matter more than the generator you choose.

There is no single best AI image generator. The right pick depends on whether you value conversation, style, licensing, control or typography. Test two or three on a real project, compare the output, and keep a human in charge of the final choice. Whatever you generate, review it for errors and label AI-made images clearly where your audience would expect it.

Are AI-generated images free to use commercially? It depends on the provider and your plan. Read the licensing terms for the tool you use, and consider vendors that publish how their models were trained if you work for clients.

Which AI image generator is best for text in images? Ideogram and ChatGPT both highlight text rendering, and Gemini lists it as a feature. Test each with your own wording and proofread the result.

Do AI images have watermarks? Some do. OpenAI adds C2PA metadata, Google adds an invisible SynthID watermark and a visible label, and Adobe attaches Content Credentials.

Can I use more than one image model without separate accounts? Yes. Platforms such as OpenArt put several models in one interface, which makes side-by-side testing easier. Check the licensing terms for each model you use.

Should I add alt text to AI-generated images? Yes, when the image carries meaning. Describe what it shows or why it is there. Purely decorative images can use an empty alt attribute, following the W3C guidance.

#10419. Apple TV has a new ASL feature, offering a richer language experience beyond captions

Apple introduced a new sign language interpretation feature on Friday, alongside the premiere of the Apple TV movie Being Heumann.

The feature, designed with native signers, offers a visual of a person on the screen. Rather than replacing captions as an accessibility option, Apple is offering another function to improve users’ viewing experience through American Sign Language and British Sign Language.

People in the Deaf community have cited inability to get the full experience of watching shows and movies due to captions that lack descriptions of tone and mood. Poorly timed captions can throw off an entire episode or movie, and incorrect language can alter the understanding of a conversation.

The new feature goes hand in hand with the 2026 biographical drama directed by Sian Heder based on the memoir Being Heumann: An Unrepentant Memoir of a Disability Rights Activist by its namesake Judith Heumann with writer Kristen Joiner.

Starring Mark Ruffalo and Dylan O’Brien, and Ruth Madeley as Heumann, the film debuted in select theaters on November 6 and was released for streaming on Apple TV today. 

A 2021 Census Bureau presentation discussed the difficulty of collecting accurate ASL-user statistics through traditional household language surveys. The Deaf community is often undercounted in national data, making it harder to measure accessibility needs. 

Apple Originals have led the industry in providing accessibility features, such as Subtitles for the Deaf and Hard of Hearing and Audio Description for blind and low-vision audiences, in multiple languages, worldwide. 

For its new feature, Apple created each interpretation with a DASL (director of artistic sign language) and an interpreter. They worked together in a studio to create high-quality sign language, capturing the tone and emotional intensity of each film being interpreted.

“I’m proud to have been part of Being Heumann and thrilled to see Apple TV supporting greater accessibility for Deaf audiences,” said Daniel Durant, who appears in the movie and also directed the film’s sign language interpretation.

#10418. This simple QR code creator is all about your privacy

QR codes are popping up everywhere these days, and for good reason. They have all kinds of practical uses, from replacing your business card and collecting cashless payments to linking to menus or information on museum exhibits. But creating one can be a pain.

Search online for “QR code creator,” and you’ll run into sluggish websites with annoying banner ads, sign-up walls, and invasive privacy policies. Some even hijack your links with their own tracking code.

It really shouldn’t be this complicated.

Fortunately, today’s tool introduces a new way to create QR codes that’s refreshingly simple—and it comes from a source with a strong track record of keeping your data private. 

This tip originally appeared in the free Cool Tools newsletter from The Intelligence. Get the next issue in your inbox and get ready to discover all sorts of awesome tech treasures!

The simplest QR code creator

A little refresher before getting to the tool itself: QR codes are those square-shaped barcodes full of little pixelated squares and a set of larger markers in the corners. You might see them in restaurants (“Leave us a review on Yelp!”), from street vendors collecting Venmo payments, or as part of the setup process for a smart home device. Most of the time, scanning them just opens a link to a web page without your having to type anything.

➜ For a simple, straightforward way to create your own QR codes with ease, check out Ente QR, a free website with no sign-ups or usage limits.

⌚ Generating a code takes mere seconds, and only a few minutes longer if you want to customize the look.

There are any number of reasons why you might find it helpful to create QR codes of your own. I keep an image file with a QR code handy on my phone, for instance, to let folks easily sign up for my newsletters. You could also have a QR code that links to your website on business cards, a printout of one that points people to a shared digital photo album for your next party, or to a page with your Wi-Fi password and other details for house guests.

✅ Whatever you want to use it for, Ente QR lets you create a code with a few simple steps:

  • Paste a link into the address field.
  • Tweak the color and visual style of the QR code.
  • Click the download button to get the QR code image as a PNG image file.

The site’s customization features strike the right balance between simplicity and utility, with a handful of dot formatting options and preset colors, plus a color picker if you want something specific. There’s also a “Logo” option that embeds an image in the middle of the QR code.

Ente says the QR code creation runs entirely in your browser, and the codes always lead directly to the link you included, with no creepy tracking in between. It’s a side project from a company that mainly works on private photo and document storage. 

The biggest limitation is that Ente’s QR codes are only for linking to web addresses. If you want to create a QR code for sharing plain text, a prefilled email, or a digital contact card, BlockSurvey’s privacy-focused QR code generator is a good alternative. While it’s not as stylish as Ente QR, it supports more data formats—but for most people’s purposes, Ente more than fits the bill.

  • Ente QR is available in any browser and works well on both desktop and mobile devices.
  • It’s free to use with no ads, sign-ups, subscriptions, or usage limits.
  • Ente does not track the URLs in the QR codes you create and does not set tracking cookies on its website.

#10415. Which MCM Has the Best Revshare? A Developer’s Guide to Evaluating Ad Partners

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

An ad partner’s revenue share looks easy to compare: keeping 90% sounds better than keeping 80%. But the percentage does not tell a developer what will happen when the integration reaches production. Extra JavaScript, unstable ad slots, opaque reporting, and difficult rollbacks can change the value of an apparently attractive deal.

For teams maintaining an advertising-funded website, choosing a Multiple Customer Management (MCM) partner is partly an engineering decision. The integration affects page templates, consent handling, third-party requests, account access, and monitoring. Those changes deserve the same scrutiny as a new analytics SDK or payment integration.

This guide explains how to compare revenue shares on a consistent basis, review integration requirements, and test an ad setup without sacrificing usability. The goal is a repeatable evaluation process, rather than a universal winner.

Google Ad Manager’s MCM system lets a parent publisher manage a child publisher’s account or delegated inventory. The commercial agreement defines the partner’s services and compensation. Before comparing offers, ask which revenue streams the quoted percentage covers and whether the reporting figure is before or after that fee.

Use three separate lines in your evaluation spreadsheet:

Revenue base: record the amount to which the partner’s percentage applies. Advertiser spending, exchange-reported revenue, and publisher earnings are different figures. Do not treat them as interchangeable.

Partner compensation: identify the percentage, fixed charges, and any optional services. Ask whether the same terms apply to every demand source and ad format.

Adjustments: distinguish estimated revenue from finalized earnings, including invalid-traffic deductions and other corrections. Document when adjustments appear and which party bears them.

A common mistake is applying the partner fee twice because a dashboard already displays net revenue. Label each exported metric before using it in a comparison.

The two delegation models have different implications for access, reporting, and payments. Google’s documentation is the starting point for checking the proposed setup.

Manage Account gives the parent edit access within the child’s account while the child retains access and permissions. Payment facilitation can allocate eligible earnings from the child’s primary Ad Exchange account, but it does not automatically cover every third-party revenue stream. Confirm the invitation’s payment percentage and the separate commercial agreement.

Manage Inventory lets the parent manage delegated inventory in its own account, without access to the child account. Reporting for that inventory sits in the parent account. Google pays the parent for the relevant inventory, and the parent pays the child according to their agreement. Ask how you will obtain reports and reconcile payments.

Before implementation, document who can change tags, ad units, consent settings, and demand configuration. Agree on access for debugging and exporting historical data. A developer should be able to trace a production request to its configuration owner.

Use this table as a request-for-information checklist. It does not rank providers or assert that any named service supports a particular implementation. Obtain current terms and technical documentation for the product you are considering.

Apply the same standards to every proposal. The following examples show what a developer should ask during evaluation; each question is relevant across providers.

MonetizeMore offers publisher monetization products, including PubGuru and Traffic Cop. When evaluating its proposal, connect the commercial discussion to concrete integration questions: which scripts will load, who owns the configuration, and how will reported earnings be reconciled?

Request a sample report showing the revenue base, partner fee, and deductions as separate fields. Check whether the proposed plan includes every service shown in the sales demonstration.

Ask for a written ownership map covering Ad Manager access, tag deployment, configuration changes, and incident response. Identify who can restore the previous setup if delivery fails.

During a trial, compare representative templates and devices. Record script requests and main-thread activity alongside net revenue, using the same measurement definitions for the existing setup.

Decision criterion: choose on measured results and documented responsibilities, rather than assuming that a quoted split predicts final earnings.

For any proposal involving a header-bidding wrapper, including one from Setupad, ask how the wrapper fits into your existing page lifecycle.

Review bidder configuration, auction timeouts, and when the ad server receives targeting information. A missing bid and an unfilled ad slot are different problems.

Check whether your team can inspect the active configuration and reproduce an issue on a test page. Agree on who approves changes to bidders or timeout values.

Measure the complete sequence: consent readiness, auction start, bid responses, ad request, and rendering. Avoid attributing every delay to the same component.

Decision criterion: the implementation should be observable enough to explain failures, with commercial terms verified separately.

When assessing Publisher Collective or another managed partner, establish how the proposed setup could be tested on a limited, agreed scope.

Ask whether rollout can be restricted to selected templates or an eligible traffic cohort. Do not assume partial testing is available until the partner confirms it.

Record device, geography, page type, and consent state so differences in traffic mix do not masquerade as a revenue improvement.

Keep a dated deployment log connecting each configuration version with the reporting period.

Decision criterion: a measured comparison should separate implementation changes from changes in audience or demand.

A proposal from AdPushup or another optimization provider may involve changes to ad placement. Review the actual proposed changes with both design and engineering.

Check spacing, responsive behavior, keyboard navigation, and whether sticky placements obscure content or controls.

Reserve space for expected ad dimensions and test what happens when no ad is returned.

Compare layout stability before and after the change.

Decision criterion: additional earnings should be assessed alongside usability and performance, with explicit acceptance criteria.

For an Ezoic proposal, as for any managed platform, start with the exact integration method offered to your site.

List required changes to scripts, plugins, caching, DNS, or delivery infrastructure, if any. Do not assume that every deployment uses the same method.

Test interactions with your consent manager, content security policy, caching rules, and existing analytics.

Document how to remove the integration and restore the prior configuration.

Decision criterion: the operational cost should be visible before the first production rollout.

When reviewing a Monumetric proposal, establish which implementation work belongs to your team and which belongs to the provider.

Ask who creates ad slots, updates templates, and validates responsive sizes.

Request a support escalation process with the diagnostic information required for an incident: URL, timestamp, device, consent state, and affected slot.

Confirm onboarding costs and payment terms in writing.

Decision criterion: routine changes and production failures should have a clear owner.

Chrome DevTools helps trace third-party requests in the Network panel and investigate long tasks in the Performance panel. Capture a baseline before deployment, then repeat the same navigation and interaction sequence after deployment. Use comparable device and network settings.

Google Publisher Console helps investigate Google Publisher Tag ad slots and delivery issues. For a Prebid-based setup, use Prebid’s debugging tools to inspect the auction path. These tools answer different questions: whether the auction behaved as expected and whether the ad server delivered the requested slot.

PageSpeed Insights provides performance diagnostics; distinguish its lab results from available field data. Add web-vitals to your own monitoring when you need measurements associated with a deployment or cohort. Track LCP, INP, and CLS alongside revenue instead of treating a single Lighthouse score as the complete user experience.

Reserve responsive space for ad slots before content arrives, and investigate shifts when empty slots collapse. SitePoint’s guide to web performance optimization explains related techniques for loading JavaScript, reducing layout work, and managing long tasks.

With the same traffic volume, revenue definition, and deduction rate, the break-even increase in pre-partner revenue is: (current publisher share ÷ new publisher share) − 1. Express shares consistently as fractions or percentages. The table below shows the required lift; it is not a forecast these thresholds only describe the arithmetic. Different ad density, audience mix, deduction rates, or reporting bases can invalidate the comparison. Normalize to the same denominator, such as revenue per thousand pageviews, and compare matched periods or properly assigned concurrent cohorts.

Assume two hypothetical setups each receive one million pageviews. Here, RPM means revenue per thousand pageviews before the partner fee. For this simplified example, deductions reduce that revenue before the publisher share is applied.

Partner A: $10 pre-partner RPM × 1,000 groups of pageviews × 0.90 after deductions × 0.90 publisher share = $8,100 net revenue.

Partner B: $12 pre-partner RPM × 1,000 groups of pageviews × 0.98 after deductions × 0.80 publisher share = $9,408 net revenue.

The difference is $1,308 for the period despite Partner B’s lower share. These are illustrative inputs, not provider performance claims. Faster payment improves cash-flow timing; it does not, by itself, increase the revenue earned.

Use Playwright with mocked responses or test creatives in a controlled environment to check slow loading, empty slots, blocked scripts, and navigation between routes. Verify that the page remains usable when the ad system fails. Automated tests should not click live advertisements or generate artificial monetized traffic.

Separate unit tests for configuration logic, integration tests for component boundaries, and browser tests for user-visible behavior. SitePoint’s explanation of unit, functional, and integration testing provides a useful foundation. Define rollback criteria before launch, keep the control configuration available, and review finalized revenue alongside performance data before expanding the deployment.

There is no universal answer from the percentage alone. Compare current written offers using the same revenue base, then evaluate finalized net earnings, performance, access, and implementation effort.

Not necessarily. Reports may differ in timezone, currency, transaction coverage, fee treatment, and finalization date. Reconcile those definitions before treating a discrepancy as an integration bug.

Ask how renewals, volume tiers, optional services, and rate changes are handled. Record the applicable terms with the configuration and reporting period used for your evaluation.

No. If deductions and the revenue base are otherwise comparable, an 80% share needs 12.5% more pre-partner revenue to match a 90% share. Measure whether that lift exists rather than assuming it.

Do not treat any protection claim as a guarantee. Ask how suspected invalid traffic is handled, what evidence is available, and how later adjustments are reflected in your reports and payments.

Choose the setup that produces verifiable net value while meeting the site’s performance and operational requirements. A good evaluation leaves your team with reproducible measurements, understandable reports, and a practical rollback plan—not just a favorable percentage.

#10414. A New York Times writer spent an hour trying to reach Walmart. Then she deleted her account and told the world

When your AI tool for customer service causes so much frustration that it’s featured in the nation’s largest newspaper, you know you’ve got a problem. That’s where Walmart finds itself this week. 

The leading brick-and-mortar retailer, and second-biggest company on earth by revenue (recently edged out by Amazon), left a New York Times writer with no choice but to cancel her Walmart account altogether.

The story of what happened is instructive. So is the solution. There’s an easy way to avoid this problem. And small businesses that do so are in a position to grab market share from the giants in their fields.

‘Over an hour attempting to get help from a human’

Ivy Liscomb is a writer for Wirecutter, an independent review site that’s part of the Times. She recently shared her all-too-familiar story of contacting a company for a customer service issue and getting caught in an endless AI loop. 

Walmart no longer carried a product she wanted, so she tried to cancel her delivery subscription online. But there was no button to do so. So she called customer support. “A bright, automated voice insisted that I could cancel my subscription online, even after I explained that I couldn’t. At some point, Walmartbot appeared to accept that I was ‘experiencing a glitch.’ And then it dropped the bomb: I could reload the page and try again, or delete my Walmart account.”

She set about trying the usual methods to get a real person on the phone—saying the right word or phrase, pressing the right buttons, even hanging up and calling back. “Finally, after spending over an hour attempting to get help from a human, I deleted my account. In an age of countless digital storefronts vying for my cart, it seemed unbelievable that such a successful brand would allow faulty AI to cost it a customer.”

She’s far from alone. Recent surveys show how critical this issue is: 87% of consumers “say it is essential for companies to provide an option to reach a human agent when using genAI,” Gartner reported. And just this week, Consumer Cellular released results of its survey of consumers 50 and older: More than 80% said they’d consider leaving a company if its automated system kept them in a loop.

Escalation is table stakes

None of this should scare companies away from using AI for the customer experience (CX). In fact, people increasingly like interfacing with AI. In the Gartner survey, half of consumers said their interactions are even easier with generative AI than they are with humans.

The key is to establish simple, rapid methods for people to break out of AI. This takes the right programming. CX tools are designed to be helpful. They’re taught to handle as many queries as possible autonomously. Usually, this pays off. They process huge amounts of data so rapidly that there’s often very little wait to bring customers from one step to the next.

But that benefit becomes a drawback when things go awry. Many AI receptionists prioritize solving problems for customers, so they keep searching for a way to do so even when they can’t find one. Think of it as a “never give up” attitude taken to an extreme.

The best AI receptionists avoid this by establishing clear protocols for multistage escalation. First, when a customer starts to express any kind of frustration, a human agent is alerted. The person oversees the interaction and tries to guide the AI voice toward the right solution. If that doesn’t work, the call is transferred instantly to a human agent, with full context provided.

This clearly was not in place for Liscomb’s calls to Walmart. In fact, she wrote, not only did the Walmart AI bot rebuff her efforts to find a real person, it also forgot her issue after every few questions.

Small and medium-size businesses: See this as an opportunity. This CX gap in the marketplace provides you with the chance to win people over. Be the organizations that provide optimal AI tools and seamless access to real people. Provide the care and solution-oriented design that people crave. 

Customers are ready and willing to leave a brand if it doesn’t keep earning their business. With the right AI answering service, you can take the lead.

The opinions expressed here by Inc.com columnists are their own, not those of Inc.com.

#10410. Don’t buy the new Apple TV 4K until Apple does these 3 things

I’m a huge fan of Apple’s digital media player, the Apple TV 4K. I’ve owned every version of the Apple TV for over a decade now, and have used Apple’s Movies store to purchase hundreds of films.

The diminutive Apple TV 4K is my sole portal to my television, and it easily beats other media streamers—including those from Roku, Amazon, and Google—when it comes to ease of use and user interface.

Like many, I had been eagerly waiting for a new Apple TV 4K, ready to upgrade. Apple’s last version came out back in 2022, and though it still works perfectly fine, I was excited to see what new modern features and improvements the 2026 model would have.

But the 2026 model, which went on sale on Friday, November 13—it kills me to say—is a letdown. The hardware is fantastic, but the device is failed by its software. And its price is double that of its predecessor. For the first time since I began buying Apple TVs more than a decade ago, I’ll be sitting this model out—and you probably should, too—until Apple does these three things.

Fixes its TV app

The worst thing about the Apple TV, ironically, has always been its TV app. That’s the app you use to access the Apple TV streaming service, as well as all the movies and TV shows you’ve purchased from the iTunes Store.

I’ve written in detail about the TV app before, and unfortunately its weakness remains, even in tvOS 27, the operating system that powers the new Apple TV 4K. It’s so barebones that it feels like the development team behind it created it as an afterthought.

The actual video playback of the TV app is fine. It’s got a nice Liquid Glass sheen and is pretty fluid. But it’s also, ostensibly, designed to be the home for all your digital entertainment—how you access all the movies and series you’ve purchased through the iTunes Store. And it’s horrible at that.

The most egregious failure (and there are many) of the TV app is that it still doesn’t offer the basic functionality of letting users organize their purchased movies and series into collections for easy categorization on the Apple TV 4K. And this is sorely needed, because the built-in Genre categories the app does offer so often misclassify or outright omit movies that it seems like a sin against cinema itself.

Adds missing apps

A second frustration with the Apple TV 4K is that it is still lacking two apps all other Apple devices support—and these apps are perfect for a television.

One is a dedicated Home app, as you have on the iPhone, iPad, Mac, and even the Apple Watch. Apple positions the Apple TV 4K as one of the central hubs of your smart home, so it’s baffling that the company hasn’t ported its Home app to it, which would let you monitor and control your security feeds and smart devices from the comfort of your couch. 

Then there is the Weather app. Apple’s Weather app is the most beautiful out there, thanks to rich graphics that visually represent local conditions. And, you know, for some 70 years now, people have been conditioned to tune into their TVs to get their local weather forecast. So why does the Apple TV, after all these years, still not have a dedicated Weather app that you can access with a click of the Siri Remote?

Expands its gaming capabilities

In advance of the new Apple TV 4K announcement, many people, including myself, speculated (and indeed, hoped) that Apple would finally turn the Apple TV 4K into a true gaming console. But when Apple released the new unit, with the powerful A19 chip inside, the company didn’t announce any new gaming capabilities to go with it.

This was surprising, since the new A19 chip is more than capable of running AAA console games, unlike the A15 chip in the prior-generation Apple TV 4K. I mean, even the A17 Pro chip in the iPhone 15 Pro, which is inferior to the A19, can run AAA titles like the Resident Evil 2 remake, Assassin’s Creed Mirage, Red Dead Redemption, Control: Ultimate Edition, Grand Theft Auto: San Andreas, and more.

Of all these gripes, the new Apple TV 4K’s lack of gaming enhancements is the most disappointing, considering that it costs $299, twice the price of the previous model with 128GB of storage, and now nearly as much as a Nintendo Switch.

Apple should have compensated users for that massive price hike—which, admittedly, was likely due to increased memory costs that were outside the company’s control—with the software enhancements above, which are entirely within Apple’s control.

At $149, these historic omissions were annoying but tolerable. At $299, they’re deal-breakers. And if you’ve got an existing Apple TV 4K, there’s no compelling reason to upgrade until Apple changes course.

#10408. Here’s how to fix the looming Social Security shortfall

The Social Security Board of Trustees announced earlier this year that everyone’s favorite government program can pay 100% of scheduled benefits until the fourth quarter of 2032. After that, the Social Security Trust Fund will be depleted, and we will only have enough money to pay a little over three-quarters of promised benefits.

(Cue the collective cynical shrug from Generation X, which has learned not to count on nice things.)

This imminent shortfall is hardly a surprise—the Social Security Administration (SSA) has been forecasting the depletion of the Trust Fund and the corresponding inability to pay out 100% of scheduled benefits for at least 16 years. Which is why the government’s refusal to propose any solutions before we run out the insolvency clock is the leading cause of ulcers in actuaries, people planning to retire in the next 10 years, and your Uncle Leo.

While there are a number of possible Social Security fixes, each one has the potential to seriously tick off various groups. That’s why we may not see real proposals for solving the shortfall until we’ve nearly hit the deadline (which is what happened back in 1983 when Social Security amendments were implemented mere weeks before the money ran out). It’s also entirely possible that Congress will enact Band-Aids that kick the issue down the road rather than solve the problem for the long term.

Understanding the most commonly proposed solutions is one of the best things you can do to help hurry along the process of fixing Social Security. Here’s what you need to know about how we might eliminate the Social Security shortfall.

How the program currently works

Social Security is more than 90 years old, which means that probably every single person reading this has never known a world without it. When a program is that deeply entrenched, it’s easy to miss important details about how it operates—and understanding the mechanics is the first step to understanding potential fixes.

To start, most Social Security funding comes from a 12.4% payroll tax on earned income, with the employee and employer each contributing 6.2%. Social Security works as a direct handover from current workers to current beneficiaries—but in years the SSA collected more in taxes than it paid out in benefits, the excess was invested in government debt (like Treasury bonds), with a guaranteed minimum interest rate of 3%. This excess is called the Social Security Trust Fund, and it’s the money that is currently running out.

Under the current system, we don’t have enough workers paying enough money into the system to ensure that beneficiaries in 2033 and beyond will receive 100% of the benefits promised to them.

What we can adjust

There are only three levers we can pull to cover the imminent shortfall:

  • Increase the amount of money paid into the program.
  • Increase the number of workers.
  • Decrease benefits.

Unfortunately, each option comes with unpopular disadvantages that could make it a political nonstarter. But if Americans understand how adjusting these three aspects of Social Security funding would work, we’ll be in a better position to negotiate a mix of solutions that will satisfy (or at least not enrage) everyone.

Increasing money paid into the program

If you’re running out of money, getting more is typically the most obvious solution to the problem. And there are several proposals for how to do this.

Raise the payroll tax

Currently, workers and employers each pay 6.2% in payroll taxes toward Social Security, for a total tax percentage of 12.4%. (Anyone who is self-employed is on the hook for the full 12.4%.)

Raising the payroll tax to 8.4% for both workers and employers—a combined rate of 16.8%—would completely eliminate the shortfall for 75 years. But getting Americans to agree to this kind of tax hike—even if it’s implemented in small stages over time—sounds about as likely as mastering time travel.

Eliminate the taxable maximum

The SSA sets an annual taxable base rate that rises every year based on average wage growth. As of 2026, this taxable maximum is set at $184,500. (It increases to $192,300 in 2027.) You pay Social Security taxes on every dollar you earn up to that base rate, but not above it.

That means the maximum anyone pays in Social Security taxes in 2026 is $11,439 (6.2% of $184,500), while their employer pays the same amount. In other words, an engineer earning $200,000 and Elon Musk both pay the same amount into Social Security.

Eliminating the taxable maximum amount could eliminate up to 73% of the Social Security shortfall for the next 75 years, according to a 2021 report by the Congressional Research Service. (The numbers may have changed somewhat in the five years since this report was published, but it remains true that getting rid of the taxable maximum will cover a large portion of the shortfall over the next three-quarters of a century.)

While this potential solution would probably gain traction among the 94% of the population whose income is below the annual taxable base rate, the 6% with higher incomes tend to have outsize political power.

Increasing the number of workers

Whether or not we tinker with the percentage of taxes paid or the taxable maximum, more workers would also help Social Security’s cash flow. But where will these new workers come from?

Raise the birth rate

To keep a stable population, a country must maintain a total fertility rate of 2.1 children for every woman. America’s fertility rate has been declining, recording its lowest-ever rate in 2024 with 1.6 births per woman. In addition to disappointing huge swaths of would-be grandparents, a declining birth rate also means we have fewer and fewer workers to pay into Social Security as those babies grow up.

Increasing America’s fertility rate would be a long-term solution to Social Security’s financial woes, but there are several stumbling blocks. The biggest is that it would take multiple decades for any initiative we enact to show up in Social Security funding. Additionally, the kinds of programs that encourage fertility, such as paid parental leave and subsidized childcare, can be politically controversial.

Encourage immigration

Immigrants, including legal residents and those who are undocumented, are a net benefit to the Social Security program. That’s because immigrants pay into the system via payroll taxes, just like any other workers, while a significant portion are not eligible to receive benefits later in life.

Since immigrants are more likely to be of working age when they arrive in the U.S., encouraging more immigration gives the economy the same boost as a higher birth rate 25 or 30 years ago. The Center on Budget and Policy Priorities reports that if annual net immigration were roughly 400,000 more people, it would reduce Social Security’s shortfall by 11%.

But immigration has been a political flashpoint for a very long time, which makes this solution a difficult one to implement.

Decreasing benefits

While no one likes the idea of reducing benefits, it is one way to lower Social Security’s costs. Although it’s exceedingly unlikely that the SSA would ever reduce benefits for current beneficiaries, there are some proposals that may affect future benefits.

Raise the retirement age

Currently, full retirement age—the age when you are entitled to your full Social Security retirement benefits—is set between 66 and 67, depending on your birth year. You may take benefits as early as 62, but the amount you receive is permanently reduced by approximately 8% per year between age 62 and your full retirement age.

Congress has already increased the retirement age once. In 1983, recognizing that the baby boom generation would begin retiring en masse as of 2011, Congress incrementally increased full retirement from age 65 to 67. This made the boomers’ retirement less expensive for Social Security, as they either received lower payments if they claimed benefits before the new retirement age, or they waited longer.

Life expectancy in the U.S. has increased over time, meaning Social Security has been asked to provide benefits for a longer period. Some experts recommend increasing the retirement age to 68 for Gen Z and/or Gen Alpha in order to reduce future costs.

However, life expectancy isn’t the same across all income levels. Lower-income workers have a shorter life expectancy and are less likely to live to retirement—and these workers also tend to rely more heavily on Social Security benefits when they do retire. Increasing the retirement age for these workers could harm the very citizens Social Security was created to protect.

Change the price index

Current Social Security beneficiaries receive an annual cost-of-living adjustment (COLA) to ensure their benefits maintain the same buying power throughout their retirement. COLA is calculated using the consumer price index (CPI), which measures the average change in prices for a basket of consumer goods.

But the CPI doesn’t account for elasticity of demand, which is a fancy way of saying that when prices go up, people change their spending habits. Which is why many experts recommend switching to the chained CPI for COLA calculations. This index accounts for spending substitutions in response to price changes, and theoretically offers a more accurate inflation index.

While this change could help relieve some of the financial pressures on Social Security, it’s an adjustment that would be felt most keenly by current beneficiaries. Imagining Nana and Pop-Pop having to subsist on ramen and tuna fish because of this change makes it a difficult adjustment to sell to the American public.

Change and compromise

It’s likely that we’ll see a combination of tweaks to our system to avert the Social Security shortfall. Raising (or eliminating) the taxable maximum and encouraging immigration, especially among higher-income immigrants, are two of the solutions that seem most likely to quickly move the needle as we decide how to handle our increased life expectancy.

Our politicians are afraid to touch Social Security’s imminent shortfall for good reason: There’s no silver bullet that will solve the problem. Each potential solution must balance the financial, political, and social costs. Understanding how these possible solutions could work can help us start the arduous process of proposing and implementing them.

#10406. Top 6 AI Video Generators in 2026: Features, Strengths, and Limits

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

A year ago, most AI video clips lasted a few seconds, had no sound and drifted off-model by the final frame. Today several tools produce 1080p or even 4K clips with synchronized audio, camera control and reference-based consistency. The market also moves quickly: OpenAI announced it was shutting down Sora in March 2026, so the list of tools worth using has changed.

This guide compares six AI video generators that developers, designers and marketers can use today. For each one you will see what it does well, where it falls short and who it suits. Plans, credits and model names change often, so confirm details on each vendor’s site before you commit.

OpenArt’s AI video generator puts a range of video models behind one interface. Its page lists models such as Veo 3.1, Kling, Seedance, Wan, Hailuo and PixVerse, so you can run the same prompt on different engines and compare the results without managing separate accounts.

Beyond text-to-video and image-to-video, it offers start and end frame control, video-to-video restyling, motion transfer from a reference clip, a character builder for consistency, lip sync and conversational editing for tasks such as swapping a background or relighting a scene. Resolution goes up to 4K on many models, with 1080p as the default, and clips are usually up to 15 seconds, with longer limits on a few models.

Strengths: model variety, a single credit pool, editing tools alongside generation and a shared library for your clips.

Limits: credit use varies by model, so it is worth testing short clips first. Commercial-use rights depend on your plan and on the model you pick, so check the pricing and terms pages.

Best for: creators and small teams that want to compare models quickly instead of committing to one.

Veo is Google DeepMind’s video model. Veo 3.1 generates sound effects, ambient noise and dialogue together with the video, supports image-to-video, first and last frame transitions, reference images for characters or objects, and outputs 1080p and 4K. You can reach it through the Gemini app, Google Flow and the Gemini API.

Strengths: audio generated with the picture, strong prompt adherence and an API that fits into developer workflows.

Limits: base clips are short, around 8 seconds, so longer scenes rely on scene extension. Dialogue quality in short segments is still being refined, and access and quotas depend on your Google plan.

Best for: developers and marketers who want audio and video from one prompt, or who plan to automate generation through an API.

Runway has been a staple of AI filmmaking since its early Gen models. Its pricing page lists Gen-4.5 and Aleph alongside partner models, and the paid plans include all video and image models, 4K upscaling and parallel generations. Higher tiers add features such as voice clones, brand kits and HDR or ProRes output.

Strengths: polished editing tools, video-to-video workflows and a professional output pipeline that suits post-production teams.

Limits: credits are consumed quickly on premium models, and on the lower paid plans they do not roll over from month to month.

Best for: video editors and agencies that need control over shots and want AI to fit into an existing editing process.

Kling from Kuaishou has built a reputation for natural motion and expressive characters. The current release, Kling 4.0, sits alongside tools such as Motion Control, a canvas workspace, an agent and MCP or CLI batch generation for teams that want to automate production.

Strengths: realistic movement, motion transfer and batch tools for producing many short clips.

Limits: the main site does not spell out all clip-length and resolution limits for each model, so check the model page you plan to use. Pricing and free credits vary by region and plan.

Best for: social video, product shots and character-driven clips where motion quality is the priority.

Luma’s Dream Machine is built on the Ray model family. Its current page lists Ray3.2 and Ray3.14, along with a “Modify video” tool that restyles footage, extends duration and reframes aspect ratios. It also lists camera-motion controls and high-quality EXR export for professional pipelines.

Strengths: reshooting or restyling existing footage, camera-motion control and pipeline-friendly export.

Limits: paid plans start at around $30 per month (or less when billed yearly), and heavy use pushes you into the higher tiers.

Best for: filmmakers and designers who want to modify and extend footage rather than only generate new clips.

Adobe Firefly offers text-to-video and image-to-video with Adobe’s own Firefly Video Model. It also provides partner models, including Google Veo 3.1, Luma Ray3, Kling and Runway Gen-4.5, so you can compare outputs from inside one product. An Assembler and AI video editor let you trim, reorder, extend and add voiceovers, music and sound effects.

Adobe states that the Firefly Video Model is trained on licensed content such as Adobe Stock and public domain material, and describes its output as safe for commercial use. Partner models may carry different terms, so read the details for whichever model you choose.

Strengths: a clear licensing story for the native model, integration with Adobe’s creative apps and an included editor.

Limits: most clips run up to 8 seconds, with some models reaching 15. Credits are allocated monthly, and premium partner models can use them faster.

Best for: brand and in-house teams that care about provenance and already work in Adobe tools.

The table summarizes what each vendor’s own pages say at the time of writing. “Entry paid plan” figures are US prices billed annually where the vendor offers that option.

Credit counts are hard to compare, so convert them to clips. Runway’s pricing page lists Gen-4.5 at 60 credits per 5-second clip, which means the 625 monthly credits on the Standard plan cover roughly ten clips. Adobe says its Standard plan’s 2,000 credits equal up to 40 five-second videos, and OpenArt’s Starter plan lists about 50 videos for 4,000 credits. Premium models cost more: the same Runway page lists Aleph 2.0 at 140 credits per 5 seconds.

Plan for waste. If you keep one usable clip out of every three attempts, your real cost per finished shot is about three times the sticker price. Test with short, low-resolution drafts, then render the winner at full quality.

Because every tool outputs short clips, the real work is assembly. A typical workflow is: write a shot list, generate two or three takes per shot, pick the best, normalize them to one format, join them and add captions and audio. FFmpeg handles the joining step from the command line:

Matching resolution, frame rate and codec before joining avoids glitches at the cut points. For character consistency across shots, reuse the same reference image in every prompt and keep descriptions of the subject identical.

If the clip ends up on your own site, treat it like any other media. Provide a poster image, load metadata only until the visitor presses play, and include captions so deaf and hard-of-hearing users, and anyone watching without sound, can follow along. The W3C’s guidance on captions and subtitles explains what to include, and the MDN video element reference covers the attributes below.

Also write a text description or transcript near the video. Search engines and screen reader users cannot see the footage, so the surrounding text is what explains it.

Short, structured prompts beat long, vague ones. Describe the elements in the order a director would:

Change one element at a time between takes so you can tell which change improved the result.

Marketing demos show the best of a tool, so run your own test. Use the same prompt, duration and aspect ratio on each tool, generate a few takes and score them against a short checklist. Keep notes on how many credits each usable clip costs.

Run the same test again with an image-to-video input if your workflow starts from product photos or illustrations. That often exposes differences in consistency that text prompts hide.

Which AI video generator is best? There is no single winner. Veo is strong for audio, Runway for editing, Kling for motion, Luma for modifying footage and Firefly for licensing clarity. A multi-model tool such as OpenArt helps you compare them.

Can AI video generators make long videos? Not in one pass. Most models create short clips, so longer videos are built by extending or stitching clips together.

Is Sora still available? OpenAI announced in March 2026 that it was shutting down the Sora app and API, so it is not a safe choice for new projects.

Can I use AI videos commercially? Often, but it depends on the plan and the underlying model. Read the current terms before publishing.

How do I keep a character consistent across clips? Reuse the same reference image, keep the subject description identical in every prompt, and use character or reference tools where the platform offers them.

Should I add captions to AI-generated video? Yes. Captions help accessibility and viewers watching without sound, and they give search engines text to index.

Do I need a powerful computer? No. These services run in the cloud, so a browser and a stable connection are enough.

The best AI video generator depends on what you make. Start with a short test prompt, compare a few tools, and keep the one that gives you usable clips at a sensible credit cost. If you are not sure where to begin, a multi-model option such as OpenArt lets you try several engines before you settle on one.

#10403. Taxing billionaires failed in California, but other states are taking steps to collect from the rich

State efforts to tax the rich did relatively well in the 2026 midterm elections, following a series of state legislative moves in that direction in recent years.

That might come as a surprise because a majority of voters rejected California’s Proposition 40. The much-publicized ballot initiative would have imposed a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of the state’s roughly 200 billionaires. Google cofounder Sergey Brin and several other billionaires spent nearly $400 million trying to persuade voters to reject it.

Emmanuel Saez, a University of California, Berkeley, economist who studies inequality and helped design Proposition 40, lamented the loss, saying: “Today oligarchy has won.”

As a law professor who recently wrote a book about wealth inequality, I have been monitoring the results of these efforts aimed at taxing the rich. Despite Proposition 40’s failure, I think it’s important to observe that many Americans expressed support during the midterms for hiking income taxes on the rich, and to a lesser extent, taxes on the second—or third or fourth—homes the very wealthy possess.

Taxing the rich at the ballot box

Taxing income is proving a more successful strategy than taxing wealth.

Major changes to income taxes were up for a vote in five states during the midterms. Three of those ballot initiatives were proposals that sought to boost income tax rates on the rich or maintain those rates. All three prevailed.

In Washington state, for example, voters backed a measure that will preserve its new 9.9% income tax on household income above $1 million. This “millionaire’s tax,” signed into law earlier in 2026, is the state’s first personal income tax.

Meanwhile, Colorado voters rejected Proposition 136, which would have capped the state’s income tax rate at 4.4%. They also approved Amendment 87, a new graduated income tax that raises rates on households and businesses with incomes over $500,000.

And even though California’s voters rejected Proposition 40, they did approve Proposition 3. That measure makes permanent the income tax rates enacted in 2012 for the state’s highest earners, which were set to expire in 2031. The surcharges, adjusted annually for inflation, start at 10.3% for incomes of $360,000 and go up to a 12.3% surcharge for taxpayers earning over $721,000.

And in August 2026, Missouri voters overwhelmingly rejected a measure that would have required the state’s lawmakers to eliminate its income tax. This would have meant losing $8.5 billion in revenue annually. The change would have let rich income taxpayers off the hook and replaced lost revenue through an increased sales tax that would have hit low-income taxpayers hardest.

The two losses were in North Carolina and Iowa. Neither state voted directly on a tax to be levied on the rich. But both approved constitutional amendments that will make it harder for the state legislatures to enact these kinds of taxes in the future. North Carolina’s governor, Josh Stein, called the amendment in his state a “millionaire protection cap.”

State legislatures raising income tax rates on high earners

Ahead of the midterms, new taxes on the rich introduced via state legislatures, rather than ballot initiatives, also emerged.

In Maine, legislators voted in April 2026 for a tax surcharge of 1% on income over $1 million. The following month, Hawaiian lawmakers created a new 13% income bracket for single taxpayers earning above $500,000 or couples filing jointly who make over $1 million. This change is paired with a reduction in rates for lower-income brackets.

And one month after that, Rhode Island enacted a surcharge for millionaires’ income to be phased in over the next three years, reaching a maximum 3% rate.

In 2009, New York became one of the first states to pass one of these high-earner income taxes. Washington, D.C., Massachusetts, and Maryland also enacted these “millionaire taxes” in 2022, 2023, and 2025, respectively.

Taxing additional homes

Another way that state and local governments are boosting the tax revenue they get from wealthy constituents is by levying special taxes on pricey homes that aren’t the owners’ primary residences. These initiatives have succeeded both in state legislatures and voting booths.

Montana lawmakers, in April 2025, approved a new tiered property tax system, which took effect on January 1, 2026. It raised property tax rates on vacation homes and short-term rentals to 1.9%, while primary residences and qualifying long-term rentals pay lower, tiered homestead rates.

New York City rolled out its “pied-à-terre tax” in July. The new tax imposes an annual surcharge of 0.8% to 1.3% on single-family homes valued at $5 million or more, and 4% to 6.5% on condos and co-ops valued at $1 million or more. The surcharge only applies to homes that are not a primary residence.

Rhode Island has a similar property tax that took effect at the same time as New York City’s. It’s an annual surcharge of $2.50 for every $500 of assessed value above $1 million that applies to non-primary residences.

And on November 3, voters in Boulder, Colorado, approved a residential vacancy tax on homes that sit empty more than half the year. The surcharge, which goes into effect in 2028, will be roughly $4,000 a year for each vacant property. It applies across the board, but homes that aren’t primary residences are the clear target.

However, just west of Boulder in Crested Butte, Colorado, a second-home tax failed. So did an effort to levy a similar surcharge in San Diego, California.

Why income taxes are attractive to voters and lawmakers

There is a good reason why taxing the income of rich people is easier to pull off than taxing their wealth: Income taxes are much easier to calculate.

Income taxes can be based on annual income tax filings, whether state or federal. It requires no extra work to value someone’s net worth. There are no such filings for wealth, except after death, if a large estate is left behind.

Wealth taxes also require the annual valuation of businesses, farmland, artwork, intellectual property, and other assets—many of which are hard to estimate.

The downside of taxing income instead of wealth is that it limits how much revenue can be raised from the people most able to pay taxes. Most wealthy people convert little of their wealth into income. One common exception occurs when they sell some of their stock.

Property taxes, like income taxes, are an exception to this rule. Calculating how much tax on real estate someone owes is easy for the authorities to do using annual municipal assessments.

What might happen next?

Despite Proposition 40’s defeat, it looks like Americans are generally open to taxing wealthy people more—at least when the states do it.

In Illinois, where a billionaire governor, JB Pritzker, easily won a third term, another interesting ballot initiative prevailed.

More than 75% of voters in Cook County, which includes Chicago and several of its suburbs, approved a nonbinding, advisory referendum asking if Illinois should adopt the “millionaire amendment for property tax relief and education.” It would levy a new surcharge of 3% on incomes over $1 million. While this win did not authorize a new tax, it revealed that support for one would be strong—at least in Chicago and Evanston.

Even billionaire Bill Gates has said he believes a “billionaire’s tax” will be necessary. The question is: What kind?

Allison Anna Tait is a professor of law at the University of Richmond.

#10402. AMD shares how it can retain 95% of server performance with just half the DRAM, sidestepping memory shortages with MEXT

Keep exploring and earning more as a member.

Reviews, benchmarks, and updates on current GPUs.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Unlock instant access to exclusive member features.

Get full access to premium articles, exclusive features and a growing list of member rewards.

MEXT offloads cold memory pages to flash storage and serves them up with a predictive AI model.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

In June, AMD overtook the predictive memory engine known as MEXT, which claims to offer upwards of 99% of the performance of a system with full DRAM capacity while running with as little as 25% of the physical DIMMs. The technology offloads cold memory pages to flash storage and uses an AI model to serve pages before they’re needed, and AMD says it plans to extend the tech across a wide swath of its IT infrastructure next year.

The pitch behind MEXT seems too good to be true. According to AMD and MEXT founder Gary Smerdon, the technology can cut the physical DRAM required in a server by 20% to 75% depending on the application and performance target. That missing memory still registers as installed DRAM to the OS. Instead of DRAM, however, MEXT uses relatively inexpensive flash storage to offload cold pages, flying them back in as they’re needed with an AI model. In some of AMD’s internal workloads, such as Synopsys PrimeTime, the company says it’s able to achieve 95% of the performance of a full server while running at 50% DRAM capacity with MEXT.

AMD has deployed MEXT internally on 145 servers, which it says will expand to 2,000 servers next year. In addition, the company has announced a partnership with HPE to bring MEXT to customers. Currently, we’re in phase 1 of the rollout, with some EPYC Venice servers carrying a “MEXT Ready” badge and a dedicated NVMe drive or bay for the offload. Phase 2 brings MEXT licenses out to these servers, as well as the RAM View application. AMD hasn’t said when Phase 2 will begin.

The AI-driven DRAM pricing surge impacts more than just gaming PCs, with enterprises also feeling the brunt of price increases, even if they aren’t running AI workloads. If MEXT is able to achieve what AMD claims, it could be transformative given the current market. Because of that, it’s worth understanding what exactly MEXT is, as well as what AMD claims it can do.

Although MEXT is exciting in concept, it’s obvious that AMD is taking a conservative approach to the rollout. Extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence, after all. The applications of MEXT are currently narrow, though AMD says it’s expanding the workloads it’s using MEXT on with promising early results.

The basic setup of MEXT is simple in concept: cold pages go to flash, AI brings those pages back as needed, and it’s as if the memory was never missing in the first place. The main problem should be obvious. Flash is orders of magnitude slower than DRAM, so streaming pages back into memory from flash as they’re needed isn’t feasible. MEXT’s trick is using an AI model to predict the pages you’ll need. And, as long as the model is able to stay ahead by at least the transfer latency from the SSD, it’s as if the physical DRAM was installed the whole time.

This isn’t a crazy concept considering how a transformer-based LLM, which MEXT uses, operates. If you’re unfamiliar with the inner workings, this open-source visualization breaks down the concept of a transformer AI model cleanly. The foundational concept is next token prediction, which underpins the design of modern LLMs. Given a set of tokens, the LLM determines which token (word, portion of a word, etc.) is most likely to come next. It makes a prediction. In the case of MEXT, it’s predicting what page is needed next, not what word comes next.

Memory offloading to flash isn’t a new concept, but MEXT founder Gary Smerdon says that AI is the critical difference in this technology. MEXT itself is deployed as a Linux kernel module that works with any Linux distro. It uses an “ensemble of AI models,” with the primary transformer-based LLM driving the technology. And critically, it doesn’t come pre-trained.

Instead, AMD says that MEXT trains in under a second when first deployed, operates on one EPYC core without a GPU, and continually trains as the workload progresses. This approach makes sense given the varied workloads that MEXT may apply to. The idea is that it would learn the access patterns of the application in order to drive that prediction engine.

MEXT isn’t perfect, but it doesn’t need to be perfect in every situation. For instance, the order of stored pages isn’t important. With text, an LLM needs to predict the correct text in the correct order, but with MEXT, the order doesn’t matter. As long as the page is in DRAM when it’s needed, that’s fine.

In order to understand the application of MEXT to different workloads, AMD has developed RAM View to go alongside the tech. It’s a memory utilization tool that shows which pages are hot and which have gone cold. As you can see from the example above, a system with 1.5 TB of memory shows near-full utilization across the full workload, but around half of the pages stored in memory haven’t been touched in five minutes or more at any given time.

AMD provided this generalized example and didn’t clarify what workload it was testing. That’s very important, as the utilization breakdown will look vastly different depending on the application(s) running on the server. Initially, AMD is applying MEXT to critical EDA applications it uses internally, such as Synopsys PrimeTime, but the company says it has focused on optimizing agentic AI, database, and media and entertainment workloads as well.

This is important not only because memory access patterns change between applications, but also because performance in those applications reacts differently when a system doesn’t have enough memory. The “memory wall,” as AMD calls it, should be a familiar concept regardless of whether you’ve ever touched a server. With MEXT, AMD says it’s trying to extend this memory wall, which may look different for different applications.

For instance, the company is confident that many workloads can reduce capacity by around 20% to 25%. As the reduction increases, however, the applications become more specialized, and the performance delta becomes greater.

AMD has shared some internal MEXT results, which look impressive, though as usual, it’s always smart to handle first-party benchmarks like this with skepticism. Starting with PrimeTime, where AMD has focused much of its attention on MEXT up to this point, it says servers running at 50% capacity retain 95% of the performance of a full server, and going down to as little as 25% capacity still maintains 80% of the application’s performance.

PrimeTime demands a lot of memory for large designs. There are some applications where performance is nearly identical, according to AMD. In a 3-node cluster running in Azure with 5th-gen EPYC CPUs, AMD says MEXT offers 99% of the performance of the full cluster while running at 50% DRAM capacity with the Spark SQL workload from the TPC-DS benchmark. SQL databases try to cache as much data as possible in memory to prevent I/O bottlenecks, creating a golden opportunity for tech like MEXT that wants to free cold pages.

Perhaps the most applicable workload at the current moment, however, is agentic AI, and AMD says MEXT has similar applications there. Across a five-agent concurrent geomean, AMD claims 99% of the performance of a full server with 50% memory capacity, and 85% of the performance with 25% capacity. With a “memory-hungry” agent, AMD claims 90% and 88% performance for 50% and 25% capacity, respectively.

The slide you can see above has footnote tags. However, AMD has not shared the footnotes with us yet, so we don’t have a view into how these tests were run. Naturally, we assume AMD has, at minimum, represented the performance of MEXT in the best light possible. We can’t do a full analysis without knowing how the tests were run, however.

What is interesting is AMD’s cautious approach to rolling out MEXT. It’s an EPYC-exclusive feature right now, though AMD left the door open for support on future products (consumer devices, such as Strix Halo) far down the road. It will be sold as a license, bundled with the RAM View software, but we don’t have a timeline on when that will happen. And, despite a partnership with HPE to push out “MEXT Ready” servers, we still don’t know when MEXT itself will be ready for deployment beyond AMD’s walls.

Given that conservative approach, there are likely pitfalls to MEXT that we’re not seeing yet, and it’s hard to imagine it will be broadly applicable to every server, at least at the 50% and 25% DRAM capacity levels that AMD showed off with its benchmarks.

However, even being able to trim 25% of a server’s DRAM capacity represents a massive cost savings in the current supply-constrained environment. If some workloads can push that to 50% capacity, that’s even better. Of course, we’ll need to see how MEXT holds up once it’s available broadly, but if AMD’s claims hold water, it could become a defining technology in data centers that can’t seem to get enough memory.

Jake Roach is the Senior CPU Analyst at Tom’s Hardware, writing reviews, news, and features about the latest consumer and workstation processors.

#10400. 7 E-commerce UX Tips for Selling Car Accessories and Home & Kitchen Products Online

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Here is a question a product page should answer in about five seconds: “Will this magnetic phone mount hold my phone with the case still on?” When the answer is hard to find, shoppers tend to open another tab instead of contacting support.

Stores that sell both car accessories and home & kitchen products face an extra challenge: two very different catalogs share one site. A car accessories buyer cares about fit, mounting and compatibility. A home & kitchen buyer cares about size, capacity and how easy the product is to clean. A single generic product page frustrates both.

This guide covers seven practical e-commerce UX tips that designers and developers can apply right away, with code snippets and a checklist at the end.

A car mount and a vegetable peeler should not share the same spec table. Keep a single reusable product page component and change only the fields based on category. The layout stays consistent, while each shopper sees the details they need.

In code, this can be a config object that your template reads from:

Showing “Not specified” instead of hiding a missing field is a small habit with a real benefit: it makes gaps in your product data visible to your own team.

Shoppers look for deal-breaker information near the price and the purchase button: fit, size and compatibility. Do not bury it in an “Additional information” tab halfway down the page.

A short comparison table also works better than three paragraphs of marketing copy, because shoppers scan rather than read. Baymard Institute’s product page research consistently finds that unclear or hard-to-find specifications are a common reason shoppers hesitate.

A responsive layout is the starting point, not the finish line. People compare car accessories in a parking lot and browse kitchen gadgets while standing in the kitchen, often with one thumb.

A phone mount on a white background says nothing about how it attaches to a dashboard. Show it in a real car, from the driver’s point of view. For home & kitchen products, place the item next to something familiar, like a coffee mug, so people can judge its size.

Good alt text matters for accessibility and for image search. Compare “phone mount” with “Magnetic phone mount fixed to a car dashboard, holding a phone in landscape mode”. The W3C alt text decision tree is a useful guide for deciding what to describe.

Keep images fast, too. Responsive sources with srcset and sizes, explicit dimensions and lazy loading help prevent layout shift and slow pages:

One caveat: do not lazy-load the main product image at the top of the page. It is usually the Largest Contentful Paint element, so web.dev advises loading it eagerly.

Shoppers often search for a problem rather than a product. Few people type “seat gap filler” the first time; they type “stuff falling between car seats”. Your search, synonyms and category names should handle both.

Mixed catalogs show why this matters. Stores that cover both vehicle and household products, such as VNSPORT.org with its separate product collections, keep the two audiences apart so that someone looking for a dashboard mount never has to scroll past kitchen tools. The principle applies to any store with more than one audience: group by the shopper’s intent, not by your supplier list.

Decorative “100% secure” badges do little. What builds trust is information shoppers can check for themselves:

At checkout, show the full cost, including shipping and taxes, before payment, let people fix mistakes easily and offer guest checkout. In Baymard’s checkout usability research, unexpected extra costs and forced account creation are among the top reasons shoppers abandon a cart.

If your support inbox gets the same question every week, the product page has a gap. Answer it on the page, close to where the decision happens, instead of on a generic help page three clicks away.

You can mark up those answers with FAQPage structured data:

A reality check: since 2023, Google shows FAQ rich results only for well-known government and health websites. Do not add FAQs just to chase a snippet. Add them because they answer real questions and help shoppers decide.

What are the most important e-commerce UX tips for a car accessories store? Show compatibility and mounting details next to the price, use in-car photos, and make sure the mobile layout works with one hand.

How should product pages differ for car accessories and home & kitchen products? Use the same layout but different spec fields. Car accessories need fit, mounting and power details. Home & kitchen products need dimensions, capacity, materials and cleaning instructions.

How big should buttons be on a mobile product page? WCAG 2.2 sets a minimum target size of 24 × 24 CSS pixels. For primary actions such as “Add to cart”, around 44 pixels is more comfortable.

Do FAQ sections still help SEO? Mostly indirectly. FAQ rich results are now limited, but clear on-page answers can match long-tail searches, reduce returns and keep shoppers on the page.

How can I reduce cart abandonment? Show total costs early, offer guest checkout, display delivery times and return terms before payment, and keep the checkout form short.

Good e-commerce UX is not about clever animations. It is about answering the shopper’s question before they have to ask it. Clear specs, honest photos, thumb-friendly controls and real FAQs turn an ordinary product page into one that helps people buy, whether they are shopping for car accessories or home & kitchen essentials.
